noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: write balanced full and ionic equations, including state symbols, for chemical reactions

be able to relate ionic and full equations, with state symbols, to observations from simple test-tube experiments, to include: i displacement reactions ii typical reactions of acids iii precipitation reactions

primer.text: Reactions are written contracts: full equations name every species, ionic equations keep only the participants. This note balances equations with state symbols, builds ionic formulae by charge cancellation, cancels spectator ions into ionic equations, and closes with the reaction types a test-tube reveals - displacement, neutralisation and precipitation.

lessons.title: Balancing with state symbols
lessons.opening: A balanced equation is the accountant's ledger of a reaction: atoms can be neither created nor destroyed, so every element must tally on both sides. This lesson walks the balancing routine from formulae to coefficients to state symbols, using magnesium burning in oxygen as the spine.
keyPoints: Balancing never changes a formula; coefficients go in front of formulae only.
Atoms tally: the count of each element must match on both sides of the arrow.
For organic combustion, balance carbon first, then hydrogen, then oxygen.
State symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) record the physical state of every species.

low.restatement: Count each kind of atom on both sides and add whole-number coefficients until the counts match.
low.analogy: Balancing is like packing two crates so each carries exactly the same mix of items - you may add more boxes, never reshape an item.
low.examPointer: The classic slip is tweaking a formula to make the counts fit; examiners penalise that instantly.

medium.restatement: Coefficients scale whole formula units, so each multiplication hits every atom in that formula; state symbols then label each species solid, liquid, gas or aqueous.
medium.analogy: Coefficients work like scaling a recipe: doubling the batch doubles every ingredient, while the recipe card itself stays untouched.
medium.examPointer: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO shows 2 mol Mg reacting with 1 mol O2; examiners ask for that mole interpretation directly.

check.stem: What must never be altered when balancing an equation?

options.text: The formulae of the reactants and products
options.explanation: Formulae are fixed; only the coefficients in front of them may change.

options.text: The coefficients in front of each formula
options.explanation: Coefficients are precisely what gets adjusted.

options.text: The number of atoms on each side
options.explanation: Equal atom counts are the goal of balancing.
The arrow stays, but that is not what balancing adjusts.

check.stem: In the balanced equation 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, what does the coefficient 2 in front of MgO tell you?

options.text: Two formula units of magnesium oxide form per reacting unit of the equation
options.explanation: The coefficient counts formula units; with the other coefficients it fixes the mole ratios 2:1:2.

options.text: Magnesium oxide contains two atoms of magnesium
options.explanation: The subscript, not the coefficient, counts atoms inside a formula.

options.text: The reaction happens twice as fast
options.explanation: Coefficients carry no rate information.
Coefficients count formula units, not grams.

check.stem: Which state symbol marks a substance dissolved in water?

options.explanation: Aqueous means dissolved in water.
(l) marks a pure liquid, not a solution.
(g) marks a gas.
(s) marks a solid.

check.stem: In combustion of an organic compound, which order of balancing does the convention recommend?

options.explanation: The standard routine settles C and H first and lets oxygen absorb the final totals.
Fixing oxygen first forces endless rework of the others.
Hydrogen first is workable but not the convention taught.

options.text: Any order, since the result is identical
options.explanation: Any order reaches the same coefficients, but the taught convention keeps working tidy.

check.stem: A student writes Mg + O2 -> MgO as 'balanced' after writing O as O2 inside the product. What is wrong?

options.text: The product formula was changed; oxygen's diatomic formula was broken to fit the balance
options.explanation: Balancing must keep MgO intact and adjust coefficients instead.
The atom counts may tally but the species written is no longer magnesium oxide.

options.text: The arrow should be an equals sign
options.explanation: Reaction arrows are standard; the fault is the altered formula.
State symbols come last; the fault is deeper.

check.stem: State the four state symbols and what each denotes.
check.modelAnswer: (s) denotes solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) a substance dissolved in water as an aqueous solution.

check.stem: List the four steps for writing a balanced equation with state symbols.
check.modelAnswer: Write the formulae of reactants and products, count the atoms of each element on both sides, balance the atoms one at a time with coefficients, then add the appropriate state symbols.

check.stem: Explain why changing a product's formula to force a balance is always wrong, even when the atom counts then agree.
check.modelAnswer: The formula identifies which substance reacts and forms; altering it describes a different reaction entirely, so a balance achieved by tampering documents chemistry that does not exist, while coefficients scale intact formula units without changing any identity.

check.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen to give magnesium oxide. Write the fully balanced equation with state symbols, given Mg and MgO are solids and oxygen is a gas.
check.modelAnswer: 2Mg (s) + O2 (g) -> 2MgO (s); the coefficient pair 2:2 keeps the 1:1 Mg-to-MgO ratio while supplying one intact O2 molecule.

lessons.title: Building ionic formulae
lessons.opening: Ionic formulae are charge ledgers: positive and negative charges must cancel to zero. This lesson uses the common-ion charge table to assemble correct formulae, from sodium chloride up to aluminium sulfate, and shows the swap-the-numbers shortcut.
keyPoints: Ionic compounds form when the total positive charge cancels the total negative charge.
Each ion is multiplied until the charge sum equals zero.
Aluminium ions (3+) need three sulfate ions (2-) to balance: Al2(SO4)3.
The charge numbers can be swapped to become the multipliers in the formula.

low.restatement: Write each ion with its charge, then scale the counts until the charges cancel to zero.
low.analogy: It is a see-saw: 3+ on one side needs three 1- weights, or two 2- weights, to sit level.
low.examPointer: Bracket the polyatomic ion before adding the subscript: sulfate arrives as (SO4)3, never SO43.

medium.restatement: The lowest common multiple of the two charge magnitudes sets the ion counts; dividing that LCM by each charge gives each subscript.
medium.analogy: Matching 3p and 2p coins to make 6p works the same way: two threes or three twos - the LCM decides the mix.
medium.examPointer: Swap-the-numbers is a legitimate shortcut: charges 3+ and 2- swap into the subscripts 2 and 3 of Al2(SO4)3.

check.stem: What is the formula of aluminium sulfate, built from Al3+ and SO42-?

options.explanation: Two 3+ ions give +6 and three 2- ions give -6: balanced.
That swaps the subscripts; charges would be +9 and -4.
One of each leaves +3 against -2, unbalanced.
The polyatomic ion needs brackets before its subscript.

check.stem: Why does an ionic formula need brackets around a polyatomic ion that carries a subscript greater than 1?

options.text: The subscript must multiply every atom inside the group, not just the last one
options.explanation: Al2(SO4)3 means two aluminium plus three complete sulfate groups; without brackets the 3 would read on the oxygen alone.

options.text: Brackets make the formula look tidy
options.explanation: The brackets carry mathematical meaning.

options.text: Brackets show the ion is charged
options.explanation: The charge is shown as a superscript on the ion itself.

options.text: Brackets are only needed for gases
options.explanation: Polyatomic ions appear in every state.

check.stem: Which pair of ions combines to give the formula Ca3(PO4)2?

options.explanation: Three 2+ ions give +6 and two 3- ions give -6.
Calcium does not form single-charge ions here.

options.text: Ca2+ and PO4-... wait, that would need six phosphates
options.explanation: That mix never cancels at six.
Phosphate is 3-, not 2-; sulfate is the 2- ion.

check.stem: Iron(III) oxide contains Fe3+ and O2-. What is its formula?

options.explanation: Two 3+ and three 2- cancel at 6.
The subscripts are swapped relative to the charges.
Charges would run +3 against -6.
Charges would run +6 against -2.

check.stem: A student writes the formula of sodium sulfate as Na(SO4)2 from Na+ and SO42-. What single correction fixes it?

options.text: Drop the subscript to give Na2SO4 - two 1+ ions cancel one 2- ion
options.explanation: Sodium needs a subscript 2 on itself, and the sulfate needs no subscript.

options.text: Add brackets and a 2 on sulfate
options.explanation: Sulfate must stay single; the sodium count is the error.
Sodium is always 1+.
The formula shows no charges anyway; the ion counts are the issue.

check.stem: State the rule for assembling an ionic formula from the two ion charges.
check.modelAnswer: Multiply each ion until the positive and negative charges sum to zero, then write the resulting counts as subscripts, bracketing polyatomic ions.

check.stem: Recall the charges of the sulfate, nitrate, hydroxide and ammonium ions.
check.modelAnswer: Sulfate is 2-, nitrate is 1-, hydroxide is 1- and ammonium is 1+, so sulfate is the only one of the four carrying a double negative charge.

check.stem: Explain why swapping the two charge numbers gives the same subscripts as the lowest-common-multiple method.
check.modelAnswer: If the charges are m+ and n-, the LCM of m and n is m x n for a coprime pair, and dividing by each charge gives n copies of the m+ ion and m copies of the n- ion - exactly the swapped numbers, as in charges 3 and 2 giving Al2(SO4)3.

check.stem: Write the formula of calcium hydroxide, formed from Ca2+ and OH-, and state the charge balance explicitly.
check.modelAnswer: Ca(OH)2: one Ca2+ supplies +2 and two OH- ions supply -2, so the charges cancel to zero with brackets preserving the hydroxide group.

lessons.title: Ionic equations and spectators
lessons.opening: In solution many ions just watch the reaction happen. This lesson separates the players from the spectators, cancels the watchers, and lands on the compact ionic equation for zinc displacing copper from its sulfate.
keyPoints: Aqueous ionic compounds dissociate into their ions before anything reacts.
Spectator ions are present on both sides unchanged and take no part in the reaction.
An ionic equation keeps only the reacting particles and cancels the spectators.
Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu is the ionic heart of the zinc and copper(II) sulfate reaction.

low.restatement: Split dissolved compounds into ions, delete any ion appearing unchanged on both sides, and what remains is the ionic equation.
low.analogy: Like trimming a group photo to the people actually shaking hands - the bystanders are cropped out.
low.examPointer: Only (aq) species split; solids and gases stay whole on both sides of the cancellation.

medium.restatement: Dissociation turns Zn + CuSO4 into Zn + Cu2+ + SO42- on one side and Zn2+ + SO42- + Cu on the other; the sulfate appears on both sides and cancels, leaving the electron-transfer skeleton.
medium.analogy: Cancelling spectators is like simplifying a fraction - the common factor drops from top and bottom and the essential ratio remains.
medium.examPointer: Charges must balance in an ionic equation too: +2 on each side of Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu.

check.stem: What is a spectator ion?

options.text: An ion present in the mixture that takes no part in the reaction
options.explanation: Spectators appear unchanged on both sides and cancel in the ionic equation.

options.text: An ion that changes oxidation state during the reaction
options.explanation: Ions that react change state; spectators do not.

options.text: An ion that makes the solution neutral
options.explanation: Neutrality is a bulk property, not the spectator criterion.

options.text: A solid that precipitates out of solution
options.explanation: The precipitate is usually the product, the opposite of a spectator.

check.stem: Which species are cancelled when Zn (s) + CuSO4 (aq) -> ZnSO4 (aq) + Cu (s) is converted to an ionic equation?

options.explanation: Sulfate sits dissolved on both sides unchanged.
Zinc is a solid metal that reacts.
Copper is the deposited product.
The sulfate appears on both sides, so cancellation applies.

check.stem: Which is the correct ionic equation for the zinc and copper(II) sulfate reaction?

options.explanation: Zinc atoms transfer two electrons to copper ions; sulfate is the spectator.
That runs the reaction backwards.
Sulfate is the spectator, not the reactant.
Charges and species are mismatched on both sides.

check.stem: In an ionic equation, which particles may appear unsplit?

options.text: Solids, liquids and gases - only aqueous species dissociate into ions
options.explanation: Dissociation applies to dissolved ionic compounds; intact phases stay whole.

options.text: Every species must be split into ions
options.explanation: Metals and gases carry no ions to split.

options.text: Only the products may stay whole
options.explanation: Splitting depends on state, not on which side the species sits.

options.text: Only charged species may appear at all
options.explanation: Neutral atoms like Zn (s) and Cu (s) belong in the equation.

check.stem: Why must charge balance as strictly as atom counts in an ionic equation?

options.text: Charge is conserved: electrons lost by one species are gained by another
options.explanation: The electron transfer leaves the total charge unchanged from side to side.

options.text: Charge balance only matters for precipitation reactions
options.explanation: Every ionic equation obeys charge conservation.

options.text: Because examiners deduct style marks otherwise
options.explanation: The requirement is physical conservation, not presentation.

options.text: It does not - atoms alone must balance
options.explanation: An unbalanced charge would violate electron conservation.

check.stem: State what happens to ionic compounds when they dissolve in aqueous solution.
check.modelAnswer: Aqueous ionic compounds dissociate into their separate positive and negative ions, which move freely through the solution.

check.stem: Outline how to derive an ionic equation from a full balanced equation.
check.modelAnswer: Split the aqueous compounds into their ions, keep solids, liquids and gases intact, then cancel the spectator ions that appear unchanged on both sides.

check.stem: Explain why the sulfate ion is a spectator in the zinc and copper(II) sulfate reaction.
check.modelAnswer: The sulfate ion exists dissolved before the reaction and remains dissolved after zinc has displaced copper, appearing identically on both sides, so it transfers no electrons and takes no part in the chemical change.

check.stem: Bromine water displaces iodine from potassium iodide: Br2 + 2KI -> I2 + 2KBr. Write the ionic equation and name the spectator.
check.modelAnswer: Br2 (aq) + 2I- (aq) -> I2 (aq) + 2Br- (aq); the potassium ion is the spectator that cancels from both sides.

lessons.title: Reading reactions from observations
lessons.opening: Test-tube observations - a colour change, a gas bubble, a silvery deposit - are the raw data a chemical equation must explain. This lesson matches displacement, neutralisation and precipitation patterns to their equations and to the hazards each implies.
keyPoints: Displacement equations show a more reactive element taking an ion's place.
Neutralisation pairs an acid with a base, giving salt and water, sometimes carbon dioxide with carbonates.
Precipitation occurs when two aqueous solutions react to form a solid product.
Ionic equations expose the reacting pair, and the reagents reveal hazards such as toxic bromine needing a fume cupboard.

low.restatement: Spot the pattern - swap, neutralise or precipitate - then match it to the equation that produces what you actually see.
low.analogy: Observations are the fingerprints; the equation is the suspect line-up that identifies the match.
low.examPointer: Name the observation and the equation together: deposit of copper plus Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu scores both marks.

medium.restatement: Each reaction type has an ionic signature: displacement swaps electrons between element and ion; neutralisation is H+ + OH- -> H2O; precipitation pairs two dissolved ions into one insoluble solid.
medium.analogy: The three types are different dance formations: a partner swap, a merger into one couple, and two soloists leaving the floor together.
medium.examPointer: Hazard questions reward equation-based reasoning: aqueous bromine is toxic and corrosive, so name the fume cupboard and nitrile gloves.

check.stem: Br2 (aq) + 2KI (aq) -> I2 (aq) + 2KBr (aq): which reaction does this displacement equation show?

options.text: Displacement, because bromine takes iodide's place
options.explanation: The more reactive halogen displaces the less reactive one from its salt.
Salt formation alone does not make a neutralisation; an acid and base must react.
Colour change here is iodine in solution, not a solid precipitate.

options.text: Combustion, because bromine is an oxidant
options.explanation: No oxide forms; the pattern is displacement.

check.stem: Which ionic equation is the signature of an acid-base neutralisation?

options.explanation: The proton meets the hydroxide to form water.
That is the carbonate variant, which additionally releases carbon dioxide.
That is a precipitation signature.
That is metal displacement.

check.stem: BaCl2 (aq) + Na2SO4 (aq) -> BaSO4 (s) + 2NaCl (aq) shows which observation?

options.text: A white solid forming as barium sulfate settles out
options.explanation: Two clear solutions react to give an insoluble white precipitate.
No gas is produced in this equation.

options.text: A solution changing from blue to colourless
options.explanation: No coloured species participates here.

options.text: The solutions simply mixing with no change
options.explanation: The insoluble product is the whole point.

check.stem: Why does aqueous bromine demand a fume cupboard and nitrile gloves in a displacement experiment?

options.text: Bromine itself is classified toxic, corrosive and environmentally harmful, and even bromine water is corrosive above 0.2 mol dm^-3
options.explanation: The reagent's hazard profile, read from the equation's species, drives the precautions.
KI is low hazard; the bromine is the risk.

options.text: Because the reaction releases hydrogen gas
options.explanation: No hydrogen forms in halogen displacement.

options.text: Because all aqueous solutions are corrosive
options.explanation: Hazard depends on the specific reagent and concentration.

check.stem: A student adds sodium carbonate to nitric acid and sees bubbling. Which ionic equation explains the gas?

options.explanation: The carbonate meets protons, releasing carbon dioxide gas.
That produces water silently, no bubbles.
Sodium nitrate stays dissolved; nothing bubbles.
Carbonates do not decompose that way in acid.

check.stem: State the defining observation of a precipitation reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Two aqueous solutions react and one product is an insoluble solid, seen as a precipitate that clouds or settles from the mixture.

check.stem: State the ionic equation for the neutralisation of any strong acid by any alkali.
check.modelAnswer: H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) -> H2O (l); the acid supplies the proton and the alkali supplies the hydroxide.

check.stem: Explain why the ionic equation is the clearer view of a precipitation reaction than the full equation.
check.modelAnswer: The full equation lists four dissolved species, but only the barium and sulfate ions actually combine into the insoluble solid; the sodium and chloride ions cancel as spectators, so the ionic equation Ba2+ + SO42- -> BaSO4 shows the chemical change alone.

check.stem: A planchet of zinc is dropped into copper(II) sulfate solution and a reddish deposit forms. Write the full equation with state symbols and the matching ionic equation, and name the observation each explains.
check.modelAnswer: Full: Zn (s) + CuSO4 (aq) -> ZnSO4 (aq) + Cu (s); ionic: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu; the reddish deposit is the copper product and the blue colour fading tracks the Cu2+ ions being consumed.

glossary.definition: An ion present unchanged on both sides of an equation that takes no part in the reaction.
An equation showing only the reacting particles, with spectator ions cancelled.
The insoluble solid formed when two aqueous solutions react.
The bracketed label (s), (l), (g) or (aq) recording a species' physical state.
